title: 28th Annual Black Hills Research Symposium
description: The Black Hills Research Symposium (BHRS) is an interdisciplinary conference to showcase undergraduate research activity in the Black Hills region. The 28th Annual BHRS is scheduled for April 1st through April 2nd, 2026. Objectives The Black Hills Research Symposium (BHRS) is a showcase for undergraduate research conducted across various disciplines at BHSU and other institutions in the Black Hills area. The symposium continues to afford students a unique opportunity to work closely with a faculty sponsor in developing a research project suitable for presentation to the public. Research as it is used by BHRS is any systematic activity designed to produce new knowledge, including new ways of understanding and viewing the world. BHRS is an academically inclusive event that values the variety of methodologies human beings use to produce knowledge. Thus any of the following activities (and more) are included in our conceptualization of research: Natural science Social and behavioral science Mathematical science Literary works, including original written works and literary analysis Artworks, including visual, auditory, and performing arts The BHRS also gives a unique opportunity to undergraduate researchers to showcase their research before presenting their research material to various National conferences like National Conference on Undergraduate Research (NCUR). For more information visit the Black Hills Research Symposium webpage.

title: Black Hills Research Symposium
description: Don't miss this awesome opportunity to hear from investigative journalist, Delia D'Ambra, the creator of CounterClock, for our 26th annual Black Hills Research Symposium's Keynote Address. Delia's talk, "From Print to Podcasting: Why Intentionality and Integrity in Your Research Matters," is sure to be entertaining and educational. Delia is an investigative journalist, writer, and storyteller who has covered gripping stories for local, national, and international audiences for more than a decade. Her curiosity, ethics, and compassionate approach to reporting have set the standard in an industry that requires a precise balance of transparency and tenacity. Delia has created, hosted, or executive-produced more than half a dozen chart-topping true-crime podcasts that are streamed by millions of listeners drawn to detailed, heart-pounding interviews. This event will be held in Meier Hall on April 2nd at 4:00 pm. Other opportunities to participate in the research symposium include stopping by Meier Hall rooms 203 and 207 between 9:00 am and 2:00 pm on April 1st to hear oral presentations from our students, and then swinging by the student union to see all the poster presentations from 3:00 - 5:00 pm. Please come support all the great research happening at BHSU!
image_alt: Delia D'Ambra sits in a gray armchair against a white background, resting her chin on her hand, wearing a gray checkered shirt, ripped black jeans, and black sneakers, with a stack of newspapers at her feet.

title: Employee Benefits Trail
description: The HR office is pleased to offer another employee benefits fair! The Employee Benefits Trail - Mapping Out What Matters Most will take place on April 1 in the Jacket Legacy Room from 10AM - 1PM. The South Dakota Retirement System, benefit providers, financial planners, and local community health and wellness providers will be available in the Jacket Legacy Room from 10AM - 1PM to meet with you regarding their products and services. Wellmark Blue Cross Blue Shield of South Dakota and flex plan benefit providers will be available to discuss insurance options. There will also be opportunities to attend an SDRS presentation. This event is a great way to learn from the experts. A drawing is planned for attending various booths and we have some exciting door prizes; you won’t want to miss out! Stay tuned for more information about our Benefits Fair!! SDRS will have retirement planners available for one-on-one appointments. If you are considering retirement in the next 5 years, are new to the system, or have other questions about your SDRS benefits, you are encouraged to meet with the Retirement Planners. Please email BHSUHumanResources@bhsu.edu, stop by in person, or call Human Resources at 642-6549 to schedule an appointment with a Retirement Planner. Seating is limited. title: Murder's in the Heir - Interactive Murder Mystery-Comedy
description: Murder's in the Heir An Audience Interactive Murder Mystery-Comedy By Billy St. John Directed by Josiah Sabrowski-Johnson A Dinner Theatre Fundraiser for Scholarships April 11, 2026 Turn the game Clue into a play and you have the masterfully entertaining Murder’s in the Heir!’ Almost every character in this hilarious mystery has the weapon, opportunity, and motive to commit the unseen murder. And it’s up to your audience to decide who actually did it! Each of the heirs to the tyrannical billionaire Simon Starkweather has the means and the motive to do away with him. Starkweather gathers his family and employees to announce the contents of his will. His lawyer, Lois van Zandt, reveals that he has bequeathed vast fortunes to his befuddled niece Fiona, her playboy son Jordan, his great-niece Paula (a Southern belle) and his grandson Simon III, as well as to his many servants. Then Lois delivers the bombshell! Within hours this will becomes invalid. Of course, the rejected heirs are not pleased, so it’s not surprising when they roam the old mansion carrying such items as an ax, a gun, and poison. Predictably, the lights go out, and Simon is discovered murdered. Simon III (played by the same actor who plays the elderly Simon) is determined to find his grandfather’s killer, with the help of detective Mike Davis. The play’s unique ending, utilizing secret ballots gathered at intermission from the audience, determines the killer in this Billy St. John maze of murder. Purchase Tickets

title: Geek Speak: A Poet's Guide to Foraging: Creating Found Poetry
description: In honor of National Poetry Month, this hands-on workshop will introduce the art of Found Poetry. Together, we’ll practice two distinct approaches, foraging from texts that already exist: the overheard, the discarded, the official and the everyday, and the overlooked. We will test how meaning shifts when language is lifted, reordered, and reframed. No prior experience is required. Bring yourself (and maybe a friend!)—and a desire to create. Presented by Dr. Courtney Huse Wika

title: Fukushima Stories - 15 Years of Resilience and Community
description: Fukushima was deeply affected by the Great East Japan Earthquake in 2011, and its communities continue to rebuild with resilience and determination. However, the realities of this recovery and the region’s unique culture remain little known outside Japan. This event will highlight Fukushima’s ongoing recovery, the strength of its people, and its rich community-based culture. In addition to learning, the event will feature hands-on experiences such as making giant sushi rolls as well as tastings of sake and food from Fukushima. Through cultural experiences and engaging presentations, come discover Fukushima today—and explore what it means to build stronger, more resilient communities for the future. Tickets are $10 per person, $5 for Under 21!
image_alt: Poster of family walking along a bridge holding hands, with Fukushima Event details across the bottom.

title: Beautify Spearfish - Trash Pick Up Day - St. Joe Street and Spearfish Creek/Rec Path
description: We are joined by The Joy Center, BHSU, and Spearfish 4-H for our first 2026 Trash Clean up! Please join us in keeping Spearfish Beautiful! Why? We have a beautiful community and beautiful planet. We have a responsibility to be kind to our planet so future generations can enjoy her like we do. We need to be the change we want to see in others. 💚 🌎 💙 🌎 💚 This month's Cleanup is Sponsored & Directed by Donald Hlava of United Country Real Estate & Ag Land Brokers. DISTANCE: approx. 1 mile from the starting point for each crew. We will clean both sides of the road. TOTAL MILEAGE CLEANED: 2 PARKING: Meet in The Joy Center parking lot We have some vests to use from the State if you'd like. If not, please wear a bright colored shirt that is easily seen. We will equip children with vests first. After all, they are our future! We will have gloves available along with trash grabbers and hand sanitizer. Buckets are courtesy of TUF Storm Restoration and Quiksigns! Feel free to bring your own gloves, hand sanitizer, and another protective gear you feel is important to your safety. Children must be supervised. Please use your best judgment on the appropriate age for your children to participate. Parents/Legal guardians are the only responsible party for their child/children's safety. Please NO pets at this event. Please respect private property - do not go through fences, open fences, or walk through yards. Thank you to our sponsors for providing the equipment needed to safely collect trash: TUF Storm Restoration QuikSigns
location: Joy (Proctor) Krautschun Alumni/Foundation Welcome Center Parking Lot

title: Breaking Silence: Know My Name Community Book Read and Panel Discussion
description: Know My Name by Chanel Miller Henry’s Books In Know My Name, the reader experiences Chanel Miller’s brilliantly-written memoir about her experience of being sexually assaulted by a Stanford University athlete and the many ways she copes and recovers from a life-altering experience. Formerly known as “Emily Doe—the unconscious intoxicated woman,” Chanel Miller comes out to the world to describe what happened after the assault, the process of sharing her story, mental health challenges, bystander awareness, creativity and coping, the legal process, toxic masculinity, and many more themes that are of fundamental concern for our community. Join us for this powerful panel featuring experts that have assisted survivors of sexual violence. Hear local panelists share their knowledge and actionable strategies for social change. Be a part of the conversation tackling social norms...you can make a difference! Please note: this event and book contains mature content and may not be suitable for all readers. Submit Questions for the panel and learn more https://www.artemishouse.org/awareness Join the Community Book Read Facebook Discussion Group in April https://www.facebook.com/groups/readwithartemis Expert Panelists Tracy Dollison Decker, The Network Against Family Violence & Sexual Assault Attorney Consultant & Advisor Rebecka Funk, LPC-MH Black Hills State University Licensed Counselor Samuel Funk, Spearfish PD Detective Jeanie Berns, Artemis House Advocate Tifanie Petro, MS Pennington County Victim Services Director

title: BHSU Senior Thesis Art Exhibit
description: Please join us on Friday, May 8th from 5:00PM to 7:00PM at the Dahl Arts Center in Rapid City, SD for the opening reception of the BHSU Senior Art Exhibition. The Black Hills State University Senior Art Exhibition offers a diverse blend of media and methodology, featuring the work of thirty-three Fine Art Seniors. These individuals represent a group of cultural advocates that are making an impact through both their artistic and educational accomplishments. Every spring this popular exhibition introduces the Black Hills State University campus and Northern Hills audiences to the work of our BHSU Senior Fine Art Students. The exhibition highlights a wide range of artistic formats and reflects the broad scope of interests by each graduating student, providing a thought-provoking experience for students, faculty, and community members. Ultimately, the Senior Exhibition catalogs a pivotal moment of many young artists graduating from Black Hills State University. This exhibition is intended to be a reference revealing connections to current students, highlighting their studio practice, while marking a meaningful step further into the art world. The exhibition celebrates senior’s exceptional curiosity, creativity, and inventiveness, focused in an area of concentration and contemplation and further situating their work within the larger discourse which characterizes the practice of art today. Showcasing student works in such a scale has been a tradition at BHSU, it is what makes the Senior Exhibition an unparalleled, seminal experience for students and the campus community. title: Join us for September Geek Speaks!
description: Geek Speak is back for fall. Please join us on Mondays at 4:00 p.m. in Jonas 110 for a new topic each week: September 14: Dr. Kyle Kopplin Designing Decisiveness – Applying Economics to High School Wrestling Rule Changes When the scoring system of a game changes, how can spectators tell if the scoreboard is simply showing different points or whether the competitors are actually choosing different strategies as they play? Without detailed play-by-play event logs, this question is surprisingly difficult to answer in sports settings. Moreover, this scenario is prevalent when policies change economic incentives and intermediate decisions are unobserved (e.g. sales tax collections, income tax filings, work promotions, academic grades, etc.). I address this problem using high school wrestling data from South Dakota over the last decade by exploiting a recent rule change and some specific features of wrestling. From there, I document how this recent scoring change induced more points scoring, promoted more decisive margins of victory, and created differences across weights, rounds, and divisions. The major takeaway is that rule changes and economic forecasts of policy should not assume static actions by those affected. September 21: Ezekiel Bucks Film as Metaphor: Utilizing Film as a Historical Narrative Source Film is a powerful source of narration. Those that fund, produce, and distribute film often have some kind of message they hope to investigate or propagate to the culture at large. Within the study of film there is conflict between who actually arbitrates this message: politicians, a self-sustaining cultural industry, artists, or consumers. Regardless of who arbitrates the narrative messages of films, film reflects the culture in which it was made and can be utilized as a historical source to understand the values, hopes, and fears of people in the past. The narrative message within film is often reflective of cultural values that may not translate directly to different spaces and times. Examining the conflicting views of film interpretation and identifying film as metaphor can equip academics and non-academic with a means to interpret the past through film which is far more accessible than other historical sources. So, bring some popcorn and let’s learn about film as a historical source! September 28: Karl Lehman and Casey Hibbert Yes And! Casey Hibbert and Karl Lehman have energized BHSU's Theater and Creative Writing programs with a spring semester class-to-class collaboration built on one simple idea that has long been the guiding principle of theater improv performance: YES, AND... Join these two instructors for a discussion of the educational, personal, creative, and professional application of this simple but challenging approach. What does it mean to always say yes and contribute to an additive experience whether you're in the classroom, at home, in the workplace, or in any of the complex (cultural, digital, political, ideological) landscapes we inhabit? Casey and Karl feel the answer is in the play, both the idea of play and the plays created in their collaboration each spring. Expect to laugh a little, play a little, and ponder a few meaningful insights about how we can all get along and have more fun. Questions? Contact Dr. Courtney Huse Wika at Courtney.HuseWika@BHSU.edu

title: Brett Kallusky || Wasteland
description: Join us for the opening reception of Wasteland, featuring the photographic work of Brett Kallusky, on Thursday, October 1, from 4–6 p.m. in the Ruddell Gallery. The exhibition explores landscape, place, and human intervention through Kallusky’s distinctive photographic practice. Please join us to celebrate the opening, meet the artist, and experience the exhibition. Wasteland, featuring the work of artist Brett Kallusky, explores the complex relationship between landscape, place, and human intervention through photography. Born in St. Paul, Minnesota, in 1975, Kallusky earned his B.F.A. in Photography from the University of Wisconsin–River Falls and his M.F.A. in Photography from Cranbrook Academy of Art. Since 2007, he has taught photography full-time while maintaining an active studio practice that investigates the visual and conceptual possibilities of the photographic medium. In Wasteland, Kallusky turns his camera toward altered and overlooked environments, revealing unexpected beauty, tension, and meaning within places shaped by human presence. The exhibition offers viewers an opportunity to reconsider the landscape around us and reflect on the ways we inhabit, transform, and perceive the world.

title: Octobers Geek Speak!
description: Geek Speak is back for fall. Please join us on Mondays at 4:00 p.m. in Jonas 110 for a new topic each week: October 5: Dr. Andrey Reznikov The Forgotten Founding Father: Noah Webster and His Dictionary Noah Webster today is mostly known – if known at all – as the compiler of the first American Dictionary of the English Language. Indeed, his dictionary is the most famous, but not his only creation. His spelling book, which sold millions of copies, created new spelling rules – rules we still use today. But that is not all. Even though Webster personally did not take part in writing of the US Constitution, his passionate political speeches and essays in support of the united country, during the time when the United States were anything but united, were a powerful influence in creating the real union of the first 13 states. Thus, he truly is the forgotten founding father – of the new country and its new culture, and his dictionary of American English is a testament to that. October 19: Dr. John Van Benthuysen A Marxist Analysis of The Texas Chainsaw Massacre Few movies strike terror in the hearts of viewers like Tobe Hooper’s 1974 masterpiece The Texas Chainsaw Massacre, but what is the ultimate source of this film’s terror? Theories for "the massacre” hold that Leatherface and his family were driven by simple criminality, sadism, mental illness, or even, perhaps, the unaccountable forces of evil. However, none of these extant theories withstands the scrutiny of Marxist analysis, which reveals the forces of capitalism, like creative destruction, class conflict, and the resulting societal alienation, as the true source of “the massacre.” Terror, in this case, has unexpected capitalist origins. October 26: Sara Freng Making Sense of What Scares Us: The Role of Libraries in Horror Films Movies are cultural artifacts that both reflect and shape the values, anxieties, and trends of their time. Although libraries are not a common cinematic setting, libraries and librarians play important roles in many horror films. Horror narratives often follow a familiar pattern: something from the past returns to haunt the present, and characters must uncover the truth in order to survive. As cultural fears evolve, so do the monsters that embody them. In these stories, libraries serve as places of knowledge and discovery, providing the historical context characters need to understand and confront the threats they face. This presentation explores how libraries function as sites of research, revelation, and empowerment in Poltergeist (1982), The Ring (2002), and It (2017), helping characters make sense of the forces that haunt them. Questions? Contact Dr. Courtney Huse Wika at Courtney.HuseWika@BHSU.edu

title: Novembers Geek Speak!
description: Geek Speak is back for fall. Please join us on Mondays at 4:00 p.m. in Jonas 110 for a new topic each week: November 2: Dr. Denice Turner A Field Guide to Faults A Field Guide to Faults invites readers into the changing landscape of love after upheaval. Through stories from A Beginner's Guide to Faults, this presentation explores the emotional terrain revealed by betrayal, fidelity, grace, and forgiveness. Rather than offering prescriptions, it offers a way of noticing—of recognizing the fault lines that run through every life and discovering how they can become places of deeper understanding, compassion, and hope. November 9: Dr. Lesleigh Owen and Oliver Johnson Some Politics of Period Poverty Why does discussing menstruation make us uncomfortable? Why are toilet paper, water, and soap provided free in public bathrooms while menstrual products are often unavailable or require purchase? Surely everyone can afford menstrual products every month... right? How does period poverty affect college students' education, health, and well-being? What would change if menstrual products were treated as necessities rather than optional consumer goods? Join Oliver Johnson and Dr. Lesleigh Owen as they explore the social, economic, and cultural dimensions of period poverty. Learn how stigma, inequality, and access shape the experiences of menstruating individuals, examine research on the impact of period poverty among college students, and discover what we are doing on campus to address this often-overlooked issue. Attendees will leave with a deeper understanding of the problem and practical ideas for creating change in their own communities. November 16: Dr. Breon Derby Knotty Habit: A Stress-Relief Workshop for Happy Hookers It is time to unplug from the endless notifications, step away from the screen, and pick up a new kind of coping mechanism: a Knotty Habit Knotty Habit is a chill, zero-pressure workshop designed to help you de-stress through fiber arts--crochet, cross-stitch, and embroidery. Learn how hands-on crafting helps with anxiety, slashes cortisol, and lets you make cool stuff. Nerd out on the science behind crafting and practice the basics at your own pace. Zero experience needed and all supplies provided. Let’s get knotty! To ensure we have enough supplies, an RSVP would be appreciated; please text 605-641-0668 Questions? Contact Dr. Courtney Huse Wika at Courtney.HuseWika@BHSU.edu

title: Pard Morrison & David Pyle: Sculpture Installation Walk
description: BHSU welcomes artist Pard Morrison for the installation of three outdoor sculptures on campus. Morrison’s visit offers students, faculty, and the campus community an opportunity to experience the installation process and engage with the artist’s work firsthand. The public is also invited to attend a co-artist talk with Pard Morrison and David Pyle, where they will discuss their creative practices, public sculpture, and the ideas behind their work. Pard Morrison is an internationally recognized artist who hand cuts and welds box-like aluminum hybrids of painting and sculpture. Morrison’s hand-brushed graphic compositions function visually as paintings. He describes the fusion of surface and medium is a metaphor for the human condition. David Pyle serves as an Instructor in the Arts Management Program at Colorado State University, where he teaches courses like Law and the Arts, Community Engagement and the Arts, and The Perfect Intersection: Art making as a Way to Learn (and Do) Anything

description: Geek Speak is back for fall. Please join us on Mondays at 4:00 p.m. in Jonas 110 for a new topic each week: October 5: Dr. Andrey Reznikov The Forgotten Founding Father: Noah Webster and His Dictionary Noah Webster today is mostly known – if known at all – as the compiler of the first American Dictionary of the English Language. Indeed, his dictionary is the most famous, but not his only creation. His spelling book, which sold millions of copies, created new spelling rules – rules we still use today. But that is not all. Even though Webster personally did not take part in writing of the US Constitution, his passionate political speeches and essays in support of the united country, during the time when the United States were anything but united, were a powerful influence in creating the real union of the first 13 states. Thus, he truly is the forgotten founding father – of the new country and its new culture, and his dictionary of American English is a testament to that. October 19: Dr. John Van Benthuysen A Marxist Analysis of The Texas Chainsaw Massacre Few movies strike terror in the hearts of viewers like Tobe Hooper’s 1974 masterpiece The Texas Chainsaw Massacre, but what is the ultimate source of this film’s terror? Theories for "the massacre” hold that Leatherface and his family were driven by simple criminality, sadism, mental illness, or even, perhaps, the unaccountable forces of evil. However, none of these extant theories withstands the scrutiny of Marxist analysis, which reveals the forces of capitalism, like creative destruction, class conflict, and the resulting societal alienation, as the true source of “the massacre.” Terror, in this case, has unexpected capitalist origins. October 26: Sara Freng Making Sense of What Scares Us: The Role of Libraries in Horror Films Movies are cultural artifacts that both reflect and shape the values, anxieties, and trends of their time. Although libraries are not a common cinematic setting, libraries and librarians play important roles in many horror films. Horror narratives often follow a familiar pattern: something from the past returns to haunt the present, and characters must uncover the truth in order to survive. As cultural fears evolve, so do the monsters that embody them. In these stories, libraries serve as places of knowledge and discovery, providing the historical context characters need to understand and confront the threats they face. This presentation explores how libraries function as sites of research, revelation, and empowerment in Poltergeist (1982), The Ring (2002), and It (2017), helping characters make sense of the forces that haunt them. Questions? Contact Dr. Courtney Huse Wika at Courtney.HuseWika@BHSU.edu

title: Dr. Lesleigh Owen and Oliver Johnson  Some Politics of Period Poverty
description: Geek Speak is back for fall. Please join us on Mondays at 4:00 p.m. in Jonas 110 for a new topic each week: November 2: Dr. Denice Turner A Field Guide to Faults A Field Guide to Faults invites readers into the changing landscape of love after upheaval. Through stories from A Beginner's Guide to Faults, this presentation explores the emotional terrain revealed by betrayal, fidelity, grace, and forgiveness. Rather than offering prescriptions, it offers a way of noticing—of recognizing the fault lines that run through every life and discovering how they can become places of deeper understanding, compassion, and hope. November 9: Dr. Lesleigh Owen and Oliver Johnson Some Politics of Period Poverty Why does discussing menstruation make us uncomfortable? Why are toilet paper, water, and soap provided free in public bathrooms while menstrual products are often unavailable or require purchase? Surely everyone can afford menstrual products every month... right? How does period poverty affect college students' education, health, and well-being? What would change if menstrual products were treated as necessities rather than optional consumer goods? Join Oliver Johnson and Dr. Lesleigh Owen as they explore the social, economic, and cultural dimensions of period poverty. Learn how stigma, inequality, and access shape the experiences of menstruating individuals, examine research on the impact of period poverty among college students, and discover what we are doing on campus to address this often-overlooked issue. Attendees will leave with a deeper understanding of the problem and practical ideas for creating change in their own communities. November 16: Dr. Breon Derby Knotty Habit: A Stress-Relief Workshop for Happy Hookers It is time to unplug from the endless notifications, step away from the screen, and pick up a new kind of coping mechanism: a Knotty Habit Knotty Habit is a chill, zero-pressure workshop designed to help you de-stress through fiber arts--crochet, cross-stitch, and embroidery. Learn how hands-on crafting helps with anxiety, slashes cortisol, and lets you make cool stuff. Nerd out on the science behind crafting and practice the basics at your own pace. Zero experience needed and all supplies provided. Let’s get knotty! To ensure we have enough supplies, an RSVP would be appreciated; please text 605-641-0668 Questions? Contact Dr. Courtney Huse Wika at Courtney.HuseWika@BHSU.edu
